headline: Town boards advanced plans for a Route 9 wastewater system and District Improvement Financing district while reviewing major residential and school development projects.
synopsis: In April 2026, town officials focused on long-term capital infrastructure, housing proposals, and local regulatory updates. The Select Board and Wastewater Study Committee progressed plans for an estimated $40 million to $50 million wastewater system along Route 9, aiming for a District Improvement Financing vote at Special Town Meeting and extending the study committee through 2027. The Southborough School Committee selected two appointees to the Elementary School Building Committee to help lead planning for the Neary School project. In housing and development, the Conservation Commission reviewed wetland impacts for proposed apartments on Southville Road and formally adopted updated land use regulations for town conservation properties. Meanwhile, the Planning Board advanced new native landscape standards and penalized an unauthorized public tree removal on Route 9, while the Select Board expanded the Senior Tax Work-Off program to 40 participants.

top_items.title: Route 9 wastewater infrastructure and financing district
top_items.why: The Select Board and Wastewater Study Committee reviewed a $40 million to $50 million wastewater plan for Route 9 and extended the planning committee's term through June 2027.
top_items.body: The Regional Wastewater Planning Committee presented a status report to the Select Board outlining a municipal wastewater collection and treatment project along Route 9 estimated between $40 million and $50 million. The project will require a 15- to 20-acre leaching area, and officials are preparing a District Improvement Financing (DIF) plan to present at fall Special Town Meeting. The Select Board voted 4-0-1 to extend the committee's charge through June 30, 2027.

top_items.title: Elementary School Building Committee appointments
top_items.why: The School Committee named Craig Williams and Heather McCloud to the building committee overseeing the Neary School project.
top_items.body: The School Committee voted 3-0 to appoint Craig Williams and Heather McCloud as its representatives to the newly formed Elementary School Building Committee. Members prioritized candidates with educational and administrative backgrounds, citing Williams' experience in school transitions and McCloud's background in classroom functionality and special education.

top_items.title: 0 Southville Road apartment development review
top_items.why: The Conservation Commission opened hearings on riverfront impacts for a proposed two-building apartment complex.
top_items.body: Apartments at Southville Road LLC submitted a Notice of Intent and Stormwater Management Permit application for two apartment buildings at 0 Southville Road. The commission and public discussed approximately 4,500 square feet of disturbance within the outer riparian riverfront area, peer review by Lucas Environmental, and the intersection between local wetland bylaws and MBTA Communities Act zoning. The hearing was continued to May 14, 2026.

top_items.title: Senior Tax Work-Off program expansion and grants policy
top_items.why: The Select Board revised the Senior Tax Work-Off program to provide 40 positions and established new oversight rules for town grants.
top_items.body: The Select Board unanimously adopted an updated Senior Tax Work-Off Policy, revising eligibility requirements and setting the program size at 40 participants. The board also unanimously approved a new Grants Management Policy to ensure that grant-funded projects receive proper administrative review and do not create unfunded operating costs or ongoing personnel obligations.

top_items.title: Conservation land use regulations adoption
top_items.why: The Conservation Commission formally adopted rules governing town-owned conservation land under Town Code Section 43-2.
top_items.body: The Conservation Commission voted 5-0 to adopt updated land use regulations governing Southborough's municipal conservation properties. The new regulations incorporated feedback from the Breakneck Hill Stewardship Committee, and commissioners noted that future amendments could address concerns such as exterior lighting shining onto conservation parcels from adjacent private properties.

top_items.title: Native plant landscaping standards for site plans
top_items.why: The Planning Board moved forward with rules requiring native plants and limiting pesticides in commercial landscape plans.
top_items.body: The Planning Board reviewed a draft policy from Open Space Preservation Commission Chair Freddie Gillespie aimed at mandating native plants, soft landings, and pollinator-friendly designs in developments subject to site plan review. Members supported restricting neonicotinoids and systemic pesticides, agreeing to draft formal native planting standards for incorporation into site plan regulations while addressing invasive species management separately.

top_items.title: Replacement penalty for unauthorized Route 9 tree removal
top_items.why: The Planning Board required a developer to provide six replacement shade trees after cutting down a public tree on Route 9 without authorization.
top_items.body: Following a joint public hearing with the tree warden, the Planning Board addressed the unauthorized removal of a public shade tree at Route 9 and Breakneck Hill Road by Capital Group Properties. The board accepted mitigation requiring the developer to donate six three-inch caliper trees to be planted by the town.
